--- title: "Autoencoders" description: "An autoencoder is a network that learns to rebuild its own input through a narrow middle, with no response to predict. On the community matrix it finds the plane that PCA finds and a little more of depth, and it shows why you report the plane rather than its axes." order: 5 categories: [neural-networks, unsupervised] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## An autoencoder learns a map without a response Every network so far in this section predicted a response. An **autoencoder** has none: it learns to rebuild its own input. That makes it an unsupervised method, like [Principal component analysis](../08-unsupervised-learning/principal-component-analysis.qmd), and it can draw the same kind of map of the stations, with bends where PCA has only straight lines. This page builds one from the passes of [Forward propagation and backpropagation](forward-and-backward.qmd), checks it against PCA, and shows what a map learned by a network can and cannot tell you. An autoencoder has two halves joined at a narrow middle. The **encoder** takes each row down to a few values, the **code**. The **decoder** rebuilds the row from the code. Training compares the rebuilt row with the input, and their mean squared difference, the **reconstruction error**, is the loss that gradient descent makes small. Nothing tells the code what to mean: whatever passes through the middle only has to be enough to rebuild the row. ::: {.diagram} ![An autoencoder in three parts. The encoder takes a row's many columns down to a few values, the code; the code places each row on a small map; the decoder rebuilds the row from the code, and the gap between the rebuilt row and the input is the reconstruction error that training makes small.](img/autoencoder.svg){fig-alt="Three cards joined by arrows. 1 Encoder, squeeze: six open input circles on the left, each joined by lines to both of two green code circles on the right; labelled input row and code. Weighted sums take each row down to a few values; many columns in, two out. 2 Code, a few values per row: a scatter plot of code value 2 against code value 1 with a large group of green points upper left and a smaller group lower right. The values place each row on a small map, like PCA's scores; nothing labels the code. 3 Decoder, rebuild and compare: the two green code circles joined to six orange output circles, each followed by a grey bar for the input and an orange bar for the rebuilt value, nearly the same length. Weighted sums rebuild the row; the gap is reconstruction error; training makes the gap small."} ::: With the identity activation of [Neurons, layers and activations](what-a-network-is.qmd), the encoder and decoder are both weighted sums, and the best code of two values spans the same plane as the first two principal components. With tanh, the code can follow a curve. The worked example tests both. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ## Worked example The data are the community matrix of *Principal component analysis*, counts of 24 taxa at each station, logged and put on a common scale by the same recipe. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() community <- load_coastal_community() taxa_only <- community |> select(starts_with("tax")) X <- recipe(~ ., data = taxa_only) |> step_log(all_numeric_predictors(), offset = 1) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |> prep() |> bake(new_data = NULL) |> as.matrix() # Each station's depth and seabed, to check the code against later stations <- community |> select(station_id) |> inner_join(select(survey, station_id, depth_m, substrate), by = "station_id") |> mutate(bottom = factor(if_else(substrate %in% c("rock", "gravel"), "Hard bottom", "Soft bottom"))) ``` ::: The autoencoder is the network of *Forward propagation and backpropagation* with the input as its own target. Its hidden layer is the code, and the activation can be switched between the identity and tanh. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} autoencoder <- function(X, code_size, activation = c("identity", "tanh"), seed = 1, steps = 3000, learning_rate = 0.3) { activation <- match.arg(activation) p <- ncol(X) n <- nrow(X) set.seed(seed) par <- list(W1 = matrix(rnorm(p * code_size, 0, 0.1), p, code_size), b1 = rep(0, code_size), W2 = matrix(rnorm(code_size * p, 0, 0.1), code_size, p), b2 = rep(0, p)) forward <- function(par) { Z1 <- sweep(X %*% par$W1, 2, par$b1, "+") code <- if (activation == "tanh") tanh(Z1) else Z1 # the encoder list(code = code, rebuilt = sweep(code %*% par$W2, 2, par$b2, "+")) # the decoder } for (step in seq_len(steps)) { f <- forward(par) d_rebuilt <- 2 * (f$rebuilt - X) / (n * p) d_code <- d_rebuilt %*% t(par$W2) d_Z1 <- if (activation == "tanh") d_code * (1 - f$code^2) else d_code par$W2 <- par$W2 - learning_rate * (t(f$code) %*% d_rebuilt) par$b2 <- par$b2 - learning_rate * colSums(d_rebuilt) par$W1 <- par$W1 - learning_rate * (t(X) %*% d_Z1) par$b1 <- par$b1 - learning_rate * colSums(d_Z1) } f <- forward(par) list(code = f$code, error = mean((f$rebuilt - X)^2)) } ``` ::: With 24 taxa and a code of two values, the encoder has 50 weights and biases and the decoder 72. ### A linear autoencoder finds the plane that PCA finds PCA's first two components rebuild each row from two scores, so they have a reconstruction error too. To check whether a code spans the same plane as the components, each component is predicted from the code's two values with linear regression: an R² of 1 for both means the code holds exactly the same information. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} components <- prcomp(X) pc_scores <- components$x[, 1:2] pca_rebuilt <- pc_scores %*% t(components$rotation[, 1:2]) linear <- autoencoder(X, 2, "identity") bent <- autoencoder(X, 2, "tanh") # The lower R² of the two components, each predicted from a code's two values plane_r2 <- function(code, target) { min(apply(target, 2, \(y) rsq_trad_vec(y, fitted(lm(y ~ code))))) } comparison <- tibble( Method = c("PCA", "Linear autoencoder", "Tanh autoencoder"), `Reconstruction error` = c(mean((X - pca_rebuilt)^2), linear$error, bent$error), `R² for the components` = c(1, plane_r2(linear$code, pc_scores), plane_r2(bent$code, pc_scores))) comparison |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 4))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Method | Reconstruction error| R² for the components| |:------------------|--------------------:|---------------------:| |PCA | 0.7056| 1.0000| |Linear autoencoder | 0.7056| 1.0000| |Tanh autoencoder | 0.7077| 0.9928|
::: ::: The linear autoencoder's reconstruction error is 0.7056, the same as PCA's 0.7056, and its code predicts both components with an R² of 1.000. From random starting weights, gradient descent found the plane that `prcomp()` computes directly. The tanh autoencoder rebuilds the rows a little less well, at 0.7077, and its code still predicts the components with an R² of 0.993: the bend found almost the same plane. ### The tanh code predicts depth a little better Reconstruction error says how well the rows are rebuilt, not whether the code is useful. A useful map places the stations by what matters about them, so each code is checked against the recorded seabed and depth, which neither method was given. Logistic regression predicts hard bottom from the two values, scored by ROC AUC, and linear regression predicts depth, scored by R². ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # What a code's two values predict about the stations predicts <- function(code, label) { frame <- tibble(value_1 = code[, 1], value_2 = code[, 2], bottom = stations$bottom, depth_m = stations$depth_m) bottom_fit <- glm(bottom ~ value_1 + value_2, data = frame, family = binomial) depth_fit <- lm(depth_m ~ value_1 + value_2, data = frame) # glm() models the second level, soft bottom, so hard bottom is 1 minus it tibble(Code = label, `Hard bottom (ROC AUC)` = roc_auc_vec(frame$bottom, 1 - fitted(bottom_fit)), `Depth (R²)` = rsq_trad_vec(frame$depth_m, fitted(depth_fit))) } usefulness <- bind_rows(predicts(pc_scores, "PCA"), predicts(bent$code, "Tanh autoencoder")) usefulness |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Code | Hard bottom (ROC AUC)| Depth (R²)| |:----------------|---------------------:|----------:| |PCA | 0.998| 0.727| |Tanh autoencoder | 0.998| 0.743|
::: ::: Both codes separate hard from soft bottom almost perfectly, with a ROC AUC of 0.998 from PCA and 0.998 from the autoencoder. On depth the tanh code is ahead, with an R² of 0.743 against 0.727. Along the depth gradient the stations bend slightly, the arch that [Principal component analysis](../08-unsupervised-learning/principal-component-analysis.qmd#pca-sees-straight-line-directions) calls the horseshoe effect, and the tanh bend follows a little of it. The gain is small because this community changes almost in straight lines, so PCA already holds nearly everything a two-value map can. ### Each seed draws different axes in the same plane The tanh autoencoder is trained five more times from different random starting weights. Each code is compared with seed 1's, and its first value with the two principal components. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} codes <- map(1:5, \(s) autoencoder(X, 2, "tanh", seed = s)$code) seed_table <- tibble( Seed = 1:5, `Plane shared with seed 1 (R²)` = map_dbl(codes, \(code) plane_r2(code, codes[[1]])), `Value 1 with PC1 (r)` = map_dbl(codes, \(code) cor(code[, 1], pc_scores[, 1])), `Value 1 with PC2 (r)` = map_dbl(codes, \(code) cor(code[, 1], pc_scores[, 2]))) seed_table |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| Seed| Plane shared with seed 1 (R²)| Value 1 with PC1 (r)| Value 1 with PC2 (r)| |----:|-----------------------------:|--------------------:|--------------------:| | 1| 1.000| 0.996| 0.021| | 2| 0.992| 0.739| -0.669| | 3| 0.999| 0.244| -0.966| | 4| 0.995| 0.473| 0.877| | 5| 0.994| 0.506| 0.858|
::: ::: Every seed finds the same plane: each code predicts seed 1's with an R² of at least 0.992, and each predicts depth equally well, with an R² between 0.742 and 0.743. The axes inside the plane are another matter. Seed 1's first value is nearly PC1 (r = 0.996), seed 3's is nearly PC2 turned the other way (r = −0.966), and seed 4's is a blend of the two (0.473 and 0.877). The plot shows the same map turned and flipped. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} shown <- c(1, 3, 4) panels <- map(shown, \(s) { tibble(value_1 = codes[[s]][, 1], value_2 = codes[[s]][, 2], bottom = stations$bottom) |> ggplot(aes(value_1, value_2, colour = bottom)) + geom_point(size = 1.2, alpha = 0.7) + scale_colour_ml() + labs(x = "Code value 1", y = "Code value 2", colour = NULL, subtitle = paste("Seed", s)) }) wrap_plots(panels, nrow = 1) + plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The stations on the two code values of three tanh autoencoders that differ only in their random start, coloured by seabed. Each panel shows the same map turned or flipped: the plane is the same, the axes drawn in it are not.](autoencoders_files/figure-html/fig-rotations-1.png){#fig-rotations fig-alt='Three scatter plots side by side, each showing the same stations in two colours for hard and soft bottom. Every panel has the same shape: a large soft-bottom group and a smaller, clearly separate hard-bottom group. The pair sits at a different angle in each panel: soft upper left and hard lower right for seed 1, soft along the top and hard at the lower left for seed 3, soft on the left and hard on the right for seed 4. Only the orientation changes.' width=1900} ::: ::: So a sentence such as "the first code value separates hard from soft bottom" is true for one seed and false for another, on the same data. *Principal component analysis* found that PCA gives a plane, not one driver per axis; an autoencoder goes further and gives different axes each run, where PCA at least returns the same ones, ordered by variance. What every run shares is the plane, so report what the code predicts, as the tables above do, and not what one of its axes means. ## Autoencoders earn their place on curved structure On this matrix PCA gave the same map at once and the same way every time, so it is the right first step. An autoencoder earns its place when the data are large and the structure is strongly curved, as in hyperspectral images, acoustic backscatter or DNA sequences; run PCA first and see how much is left to find. The reconstruction error is useful on its own too: a row that rebuilds badly is unlike the rows the network learned from, which makes autoencoders a common way to flag unusual records, such as a faulty sensor reading. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The maths, if you want it With the identity activation and centred columns, the autoencoder rebuilds $X$ as $X W_1 W_2$ and minimises $\lVert X - X W_1 W_2 \rVert^2$. The product $W_1 W_2$ has rank at most $k$, the code size, and the best rank-$k$ approximation of $X$ is its projection onto the first $k$ principal components, $X V_k V_k^\top$, where $V_k$ holds their loadings (the Eckart–Young theorem). So at the minimum the code $X W_1$ spans the same plane as the first $k$ components. The weights are not unique: $W_1 = V_k A$ and $W_2 = A^{-1} V_k^\top$ give the same reconstruction for any invertible $k \times k$ matrix $A$, which turns, stretches or flips the axes. That is why the axes depend on the random start and the plane does not. ::: ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - An **autoencoder** learns to rebuild its own input through a narrow middle. The values in the middle are the **code**, and the loss is the **reconstruction error**. - A linear autoencoder is PCA. Its reconstruction error matched PCA's, 0.7056, and its code predicted both principal components with an R² of 1.000. - With tanh, the code predicted depth a little better than PCA's two components, an R² of 0.743 against 0.727. The community changes almost in straight lines, so a bend has little to add. - Every seed found the same plane and different axes in it. Report what the code predicts, not what one of its axes means. - Run PCA first. Autoencoders earn their place on large data with curved structure, and their reconstruction error flags unusual rows. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Give PCA and the linear autoencoder a code of three values (`components$x[, 1:3]` and `autoencoder(X, 3, "identity")`). Do their reconstruction errors still match, and how far does the error fall from two values? 2. Shuffle each column of `X` on its own, the baseline of [How many components to keep](../08-unsupervised-learning/dimensionality-reduction.qmd), and train the tanh autoencoder on the shuffled matrix. How much higher is its reconstruction error than on the real one, and what does the gap say about the structure in the community?
